extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys/agents, and patent examiners in the Republic of Korea
extracted.subtask_description: Korean Intellectual Property Office guidelines for (1) when and how an applicant may claim that a disclosure should not be considered prior art under Article 30, and (2) how examiners determine inventive step under Article 29(2). Covers formal and substantive examination procedures, evidentiary requirements, and concrete obviousness factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of intention to invoke Article 30 at filing
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant shall state, when filing the application, that the person intends to take advantage from the provision of Article 30 paragraph (1) subparagraph (1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written intention must be included in the application filing; failure to state intent may affect eligibility to rely on Article 30.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission deadline for documents proving Article 30 applicability (domestic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant shall submit documents proving the fact that the provision of Article 30 applies to the invention, within thirty days of the date of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents must be timely submitted within 30 days of filing to support the Article 30 claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission deadline for international applications (critical date rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an international patent application, a person intending to take advantage of Article 30 shall state their intention in the application and submit the documents proving the intention within thirty days after the critical date (the date for submitting domestic documents) as prescribed in Article 201 paragraph (4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International/PCT-route applicants follow the critical-date timing (see Article 200 Patent Act and Special provisions) rather than the domestic 30‑day-from-filing rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof that the discloser is the person with right to apply
rubrics_metrics.description: It shall be proved that a person who disclosed an invention is the person who has the right to apply for a patent. Where the person who disclosed the invention is not the inventor or applicant, the applicant shall submit documents proving that, when displaying the invention, he or she is a successor to the person with the right to apply for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the discloser differs from inventor/applicant, documentary evidence of succession/assignment or other right must be provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of disclosure against the right‑holder's intention
rubrics_metrics.description: A person intending to take advantage of Article 30 shall prove that the invention is disclosed or used against the intention of the person with the right to apply for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims and proofs that the invention was publicly known against intention are judged case by case; various types of evidence may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formality examination for Article 30 claims (timing and discloser identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: KIPO conducts a formality examination to identify whether the application is filed within twelve months (six months in case of filing date being earlier than March 15, 2012) of the date on which the invention is publicly known and whether the invention is publicly known by a person with the right to apply for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the publicly known invention is identical to the filed invention is for substantive examination. KIPO may invite complementary documents where identification of the displayed invention or exhibition details is difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completing documentary evidence on exhibitions/public displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a person submits a document proving that an invention is displayed at an exhibition, if it is difficult to identify the invention displayed, the Office may invite the applicant to submit a complementary document to identify the fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If organizer, title, date, or venue are in doubt, the Office may ask for additional proof such as catalogs, photos, or certificates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for notice to correct defects in Article 30 claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding the submission of the written intention, the office gives the applicant a notice to correct defects when: (a) the discloser is different from the filer/inventor; (b) the application is filed more than 12 months (6 months pre-2012) after the disclosure date; (c) wrong disclosure date/type or incorrect information on supporting documents; (d) submitted documents are not enough to prove the relevant fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated defects trigger a formal notice to correct; if not corrected within the designated period, the Article 30 claiming procedure may be invalidated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence of failure to correct Article 30 defects
rubrics_metrics.description: When the applicant does not make an amendment within a designated period after notification, the office invalidates the claiming procedure under Article 30 (in this case, the filing procedure is effective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to cure formal defects means the Article 30 claim is rejected; the filing remains effective but the protection from the disclosure is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial examination treatment of Article 30 disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner reviews submitted documents and examines the invention; disclosures that fall under any of the provisions of Article 30 are recognized as non‑prior art in the examination where Article 29 paragraph (1) or (2) applies to the invention claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claiming procedure fails because defects are found in the application and documents, the submitted documents may be used as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inseparably related multiple disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person with right discloses an invention several times before filing, Article 30 may apply to all acts of disclosure if the acting is legitimately applied to Article 30 paragraph (1) subparagraph (1); if an act of disclosure is inseparably related to other disclosures, applicant may be exempted from submitting proof for the second and subsequent disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 12‑month period is calculated from the earliest date of publication. Examples of inseparable disclosures include multi‑day examinations, distributed explanations on examination date, first/second editions of a publication, collections and oral presentations, lecture and booklet, lecture tours, exhibition display and catalog.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third‑person public disclosure between applicant's disclosure and filing
rubrics_metrics.description: If another (B) laid open the same invention between the applicant's disclosure (A) and filing date of A, the examiner shall refuse application A for lack of novelty, except where it is obvious that B's laying open was made by learning from disclosure A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After issuing reasons for refusal, the examiner will refuse if the applicant cannot establish that the third person learned from the applicant's disclosure or that the invention was filed against the applicant's intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous filings on same date (Article 36 procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicant A files within 12 months and took advantage of Article 30, and on the same filing date a third person files B with the same invention, Article 36 paragraph (2) applies to A and B: they are related and applicants should reach an agreement on who will obtain a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should instruct consultation under Article 36(6) rather than immediately refusing B for lack of novelty; only the person agreed upon by all applicants may obtain the patent; if B withdraws, A may obtain patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of applicant's own application in patent gazette excludes Article 30
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent application is filed by a person with the right and the application is published in the patent gazette, Article 30 does not apply to the invention (the laying open is not voluntary disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Office mistakenly lays open an application before completion of filing procedure, that disclosure may be regarded as against the applicant's intention and Article 30 may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing rules for priority claims and Article 30
rubrics_metrics.description: When filing an application claiming priority under a relevant treaty, to take advantage of Article 30 the applicant shall file in the Republic of Korea within 12 months (6 months pre‑Mar 15, 2012) of the acting date to which Article 30 applies. Exception: if earlier KIPO application (priority basis) was filed within 12 months of publication, Article 30 may still apply even if subsequent application is outside 12 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants relying on priority must ensure the appropriate Korean filing within the statutory periods to benefit from Article 30.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third‑party disclosure by request or with permission (implied consent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 30 paragraph (1) subparagraph (1) also applies when (a) the right‑holder asks a third person to disclose an invention and it is disclosed by the third person, or (b) the third person discloses after obtaining permission (implied consent is approved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case (a) includes when right‑holder commits disclosure to a third person (even if name not stated) and must prove the right‑holder relationship; press releases/scripts to newspapers and subsequent disclosures are included but require proof the sender was right‑holder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third‑party references that explicitly identify inventor/company
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure where a person without the right clarifies the inventor or the company for which the inventor works and refers to the invention is covered by Article 30 (i.e., a third person referring to the invention of the right‑holder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Company disclosures such as catalogs that reveal the invention may be treated as disclosures attributed to right‑holder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint inventors/presenters rule for Article 30
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more persons jointly make an invention or file an application, if among presenters who disclosed the invention at least one person is the same as the inventor or applicant, Article 30 may apply without need to prove that the inventor/applicant is the person who disclosed the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no relation exists between inventor/applicant and the discloser, the applicant must submit (i) document proving the presenter is the person with right; (ii) document proving disclosure was by request of the right‑holder; (iii) document proving presenter obtained permission to refer to the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step statutory standard (Article 29(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding paragraph (1), if an invention could have been easily made, before the filing, by a person skilled in the art based on an invention(s) referred to in paragraph (1), a patent may not be granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive step is not defined in the Act; the guideline explains it as absence when invention could have been easily made by a person skilled in the art from prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purport of inventive step requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The purport is not to grant patents to inventions that could have been easily made by a person skilled in the art, because granting patents to slightly advanced arts hampers technological progress and gives exclusive rights to essentially the same prior arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames inventive step as a threshold to prevent monopolies on trivial advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'prior to filing' (precise filing time)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Prior to filing of a patent application' refers to the definite time, in hours and minutes at the time of filing (local Korean time). If a disclosure abroad precedes the Korean filing time, it is considered cited invention under Article 29(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners consider exact filing timestamps when comparing foreign/public disclosures to the filing instant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothetical person who has common general knowledge in the art, ability to use ordinary technical means (experiments, analysis, manufacture), ability to exercise ordinary creativity in selecting materials/changing designs, and can comprehend all technical matters regarding the state of the art at time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also described as an expert able to comprehend technical matters relevant to the problem solved by the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the 'state of the art' for inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the art includes inventions referred to in Article 29(1), common general knowledge, and other publicly known technical matters, including ordinary methods for daily works and experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All relevant technical information in the field of the claimed invention at filing time is part of the state of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'could have been easily made'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Could have been easily made by a person skilled in the art' means whether such a person could have easily conceived the invention by exercising ordinary creativity or based on motivation induced from prior inventions/publications prior to filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inquiry centers on whether claimed subject matter is a mere matter of routine design or motivated combination of prior teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per‑claim assessment of inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are two or more claims in an application, the determination of inventive step should be made for each claim separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must evaluate inventive step claim‑by‑claim; refusals should point to the specific claim and the reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequencing: novelty determination before inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of novelty should come first; inventive step determination is distinct and based on whether claimed invention could have been easily made even if novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an invention is not novel, examiner may nonetheless notify reasons for refusal on inventive step, but novelty is assessed first (citing Supreme Court decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's comprehensive approach to inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner shall consider the overall state of the art, the purpose, technical structure, advantageous effects, applicant's opinion, and focus on the difficulty of the technical structure to comprehensively determine inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key considerations: (1) whether cited prior art provides motivation, (2) whether differences are mere exercise of ordinary creativity, (3) whether claimed invention has advantageous effects over cited art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to determine inventive step (four steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Specify the claimed invention (same as novelty). (2) Specify cited inventions (from viewpoint of person skilled in art). (3) Choose closest cited invention and clearly identify differences; treat structurally combined elements as one integrated unit. (4) Determine whether the claimed invention could have been easily made in view of cited inventions or common general knowledge before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The selection of the closest cited invention and accurate comparison (especially integrated structural elements) is critical to the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of cited inventions – technical field relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: A cited invention should, in principle, be selected from the same technical field or a reasonably relevant technical field to the problem, effect, and use of the claimed invention; technical field can be inferred from effects or functions of claim elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art from different fields can be cited when it might be applied to solve the problem or used by a skilled person; relevance, similarity of problem, and similarity of function/operation are considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and selection of 'closest cited invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The closest cited invention' means the most relevant among selected cited inventions that a person skilled in the art would choose and which discloses most of the technical features of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer choosing from proximate technical fields or inventions sharing same effect, use, or technical problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineligible cited references where conception is precluded
rubrics_metrics.description: When a cited reference describes the technical idea such that the claimed invention's technical idea cannot be easily conceived, that cited reference is not eligible as a cited invention; however, eligibility remains if the claimed idea can be arrived at via other aspects (e.g., field relation, similarity of function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner weighs whether the cited disclosure would have actually led a skilled person to the claimed invention; mere presence in prior art is not sufficient if it precludes the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant admissions may be used as cited invention
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant admits in the specification that a technology is publicly known prior to filing, that technology may properly be selected as a cited invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self‑admissions in the specification can be used against inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incomplete prior art can be cited
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the prior art constitutes an incomplete invention (e.g., insufficient experimental proof), it can be cited in determining inventive step if a person skilled in the art can recognize the relevant technical fact or effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an incomplete pharmaceutical disclosure may still supply motivation to try known compounds if not contrary to technical common sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable cause/motivation grounds for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong grounds that a skilled person would be led to the claimed invention include suggestions shown in cited disclosures, close similarity of problem to be solved, close similarity of function/work/operation, and close relevance of technical fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors support an obviousness conclusion when they would have motivated a skilled person to combine or adapt prior teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestions in cited disclosures as evidence of motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions shown in the disclosures of the cited inventions relevant to a claimed invention can be strong grounds for determining that a skilled person would have been led to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit or explicit teachings that point toward the claimed modification/support a finding of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close similarity of problem as ground for combining prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: If the technical problems of claimed and cited inventions are closely similar, that can be a strong ground for determining that a skilled person would combine cited inventions and arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner assesses whether problems are sufficiently similar or whether common technical sense makes the combination obvious even across fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different problems may still yield obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if cited inventions address different problems, if it is obvious that a skilled person could arrive at the claimed invention by mere exercise of ordinary creativity, inventive step can be denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include transferring features from one context (metal disk brakes) to another (carbon disk brakes) when routine adaptation suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close similarity of function/work/operation as ground
rubrics_metrics.description: A close similarity in function, work, or operation between claimed and cited inventions (or between cited inventions) can be a well‑founded ground that a skilled person would reach the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application of a known functional part from one device to another with similar operation may be considered obvious.
